claim: Attempts to harness T cell cytotoxic capacity as a therapy have met limited efficacy, partially as a result of the suppressive microenvironment which limits their migration and activation.
source: Despite the central role of T cells in tumor immunity, attempts to harness their cytotoxic capacity as a therapy have met limited efficacy, partially as a result of the suppressive microenvironment which limits their migration and activation.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about T cell therapy limitations in the abstract.

claim: Myeloid cells massively infiltrate tumors and are well adapted to survive harsh conditions.
source: In contrast, myeloid cells massively infiltrate tumors and are well adapted to survive these harsh conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Myeloid cells often adopt an immunosuppressive phenotype upon migration to tumors.
source: While they are equipped with cell-killing abilities, they often adopt an immunosuppressive phenotype upon migration to tumors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Activation of IgM-induced signaling in murine myeloid cells results in secretion of lytic granules and massive tumor cell death.
source: Here, we found that activation of IgM-induced signaling in murine myeloid cells results in secretion of lytic granules and massive tumor cell death.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Myeloid cells do not express the antibody-derived portion used to recognize the tumor antigen due to the induction of an ER stress response.
source: Nonetheless, we found that myeloid cells do not express the antibody-derived portion used to recognize the tumor antigen due to the induction of an ER stress response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-4.

claim: Incubation of macrophages expressing modified FcγRI receptors along with tumor-binding IgG induced massive tumor cell killing and secretion of reactive oxygen species and Granzyme B.
source: Incubation of macrophages expressing these receptors along with tumor-binding IgG induced massive tumor cell killing and secretion of reactive oxygen species and Granzyme B.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: A high prevalence of tumor-infiltrating T cells is associated with improved prognosis and survival.
source: While a high prevalence of tumor-infiltrating T cells is associated with improved prognosis and survival (Thorsson et al., 2018; Bruni et al., 2020), infiltration of myeloid cells is often associated with poor prognosis and tumor refractory (Greten and Grivennikov, 2019; Hanahan and Coussens, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Infiltration of myeloid cells is often associated with poor prognosis and tumor refractory.
source: While a high prevalence of tumor-infiltrating T cells is associated with improved prognosis and survival (Thorsson et al., 2018; Bruni et al., 2020), infiltration of myeloid cells is often associated with poor prognosis and tumor refractory (Greten and Grivennikov, 2019; Hanahan and Coussens, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tumor-reactive T cells generated spontaneously by the host bear low to moderate affinity (10–4M- 10–6M).
source: In most cases however, tumor-reactive T cells generated spontaneously by the host bear low to moderate affinity (10–4M- 10–6M) (Hoffmann and Slansky, 2020; Reuben et al., 2020), which is below the activation threshold needed for therapeutic effect, and attempts to increase TCR affinity using genetical engineering are often limited by induction of cross-reactivity (Johnson et al., 2009; Casucci et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The affinity of spontaneously generated tumor-reactive T cells is below the activation threshold needed for therapeutic effect.
source: In most cases however, tumor-reactive T cells generated spontaneously by the host bear low to moderate affinity (10–4M- 10–6M) (Hoffmann and Slansky, 2020; Reuben et al., 2020), which is below the activation threshold needed for therapeutic effect, and attempts to increase TCR affinity using genetical engineering are often limited by induction of cross-reactivity (Johnson et al., 2009; Casucci et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents an inference from the affinity data.

claim: Attempts to increase TCR affinity using genetical engineering are often limited by induction of cross-reactivity.
source: In most cases however, tumor-reactive T cells generated spontaneously by the host bear low to moderate affinity (10–4M- 10–6M) (Hoffmann and Slansky, 2020; Reuben et al., 2020), which is below the activation threshold needed for therapeutic effect, and attempts to increase TCR affinity using genetical engineering are often limited by induction of cross-reactivity (Johnson et al., 2009; Casucci et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CAR T cell therapy has been proven remarkably successful in treating liquid tumors.
source: Indeed, this strategy benefits from overcoming the complex, multistep, and highly regulated activation process of T cells (June et al., 2014; Gross and Eshhar, 2016) and has been proven remarkably successful in treating liquid tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The harsh microenvironment characterizing solid tumors manifests a major limitation to T-cell-based treatments.
source: However, the harsh microenvironment characterizing solid tumors manifests a major limitation to T-cell-based treatments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Hypoxic and acidic conditions at tumor sites, along with immunosuppressive capacity of tumor cells limit T cell infiltration, survival, and cytotoxicity.
source: Hypoxic and acidic conditions at tumor sites, along with immunosuppressive capacity of tumor cells limit T cell infiltration, survival, and cytotoxicity (Joyce and Fearon, 2015; Hanley and Thomas, 2020; Lim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myeloid cells migrate efficiently into the tumor mass and are well adapted to survive and function under harsh environment.
source: In contrast to T cells, myeloid cells migrate efficiently into the tumor mass and are well adapted to survive and function under this harsh environment (Bruni et al., 2020; Greten and Grivennikov, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myeloid cells acquire an immunosuppressive phenotype once in the vicinity of the tumor cells and promote tumor growth.
source: However, while myeloid cells are potentially able to produce cytotoxic compounds, they acquire an immunosuppressive phenotype once in the vicinity of the tumor cells and promote tumor growth (Grivennikov et al., 2010; Mantovani and Sica, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MHC-matched allogeneic tumors, which spontaneously regressed, are coated with IgG and IgM antibodies soon after tumor initiation.
source: We have previously demonstrated that MHC-matched allogeneic tumors, which spontaneously regressed, are coated with IgG and IgM antibodies soon after tumor initiation and are found in proximity to tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells (Carmi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Tumor-binding IgG and IgM antibodies are found in proximity to tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells.
source: We have previously demonstrated that MHC-matched allogeneic tumors, which spontaneously regressed, are coated with IgG and IgM antibodies soon after tumor initiation and are found in proximity to tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells (Carmi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Incubation of MoDC with IgG-IC, but not with IgM-IC, induced T cell immunity and prevented tumor growth.
source: We found that incubation of MoDC with IgG-IC, but not with IgM-IC, induced T cell immunity and prevented tumor growth (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Incubation in vitro of MoDC with tumor cells coated with allogenic IgM but not with IgG, resulted in a massive killing of the tumor cells.
source: We noticed however, that incubation in vitro of MoDC with tumor cells coated with allogenic IgM but not with IgG, resulted in a massive killing of the tumor cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Significantly higher levels of both GrB and NO were detected upon incubation with allogenic IgM-IC.
source: Consistent with their killing rates, significantly higher levels of both GrB and NO were detected upon incubation with allogenic IgM-IC (Figure 1D), indicating that both secretion of reactive oxygen species and lysosome deposition are involved in the killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both secretion of reactive oxygen species and lysosome deposition are involved in the killing induced by IgM-IC.
source: Consistent with their killing rates, significantly higher levels of both GrB and NO were detected upon incubation with allogenic IgM-IC (Figure 1D), indicating that both secretion of reactive oxygen species and lysosome deposition are involved in the killing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GrB and NO data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Activation with IgG-IC induced classical singling through Fcγ receptors, characterized by high levels of TNFα and IL12, and activation of enzymes in the MAP kinase pathway.
source: Activation with IgG-IC induced classical singling through Fcγ receptors, characterized by high levels of TNFα and IL12, and activation of enzymes in the MAP kinase pathway (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: The phenotype of IgM-IC activated MoDC was characterized by low levels of TNFα and high IL-12.
source: The phenotype of IgM-IC activated MoDC was more complicated and characterized by low levels of TNFα and high IL-12, suggesting that Akt was only partially phosphorylated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: IgM-IC activation resulted in only neglectable levels of Akt phosphorylation.
source: Flow cytometric analysis indicated only neglectable levels of Akt phosphorylation, while ERK and p38 phosphorylation was comparable to that induced by IgG-IC along with higher levels of phospho-JNK (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: ERK and p38 phosphorylation induced by IgM-IC was comparable to that induced by IgG-IC.
source: Flow cytometric analysis indicated only neglectable levels of Akt phosphorylation, while ERK and p38 phosphorylation was comparable to that induced by IgG-IC along with higher levels of phospho-JNK (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: IgM-IC activation resulted in higher levels of phospho-JNK compared to IgG-IC.
source: Flow cytometric analysis indicated only neglectable levels of Akt phosphorylation, while ERK and p38 phosphorylation was comparable to that induced by IgG-IC along with higher levels of phospho-JNK (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: The signaling cascade induced by IgM most likely indicates a combination of several signaling chains recruited by IgM, including Fcγ and C1q receptors.
source: This somewhat unique signaling cascade most likely indicates a combination of several signaling chains recruited by IgM, including Fcγ and C1q receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the signaling data.

claim: All CAR constructs were expressed on cell membrane within 24 hr in HEK 293 FT cells.
source: Indeed, all constructs were expressed on cell membrane within 24 hr (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: About 30% of DC2.4 and RAW 264.7 cells expressed mCherry control plasmid.
source: In both cell lines, about 30% of the cells expressed mCherry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: No CAR construct expression was detected in DC2.4 and RAW 264.7 myeloid cells by either confocal microscopy or flow cytometric analysis.
source: In sharp contrast, however, we were unable to detect any construct expression in myeloid cells by either confocal microscopy or flow cytometric analysis (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No CAR expression was detected in THP-1 monocyte cell line.
source: Consistent with our results using mouse cells, we could not detect any CAR expression in THP-1 cells, while in Jurakt cells their expression was comparable to mCherry transfection rates (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: CAR expression in Jurkat T cells was comparable to mCherry transfection rates.
source: Consistent with our results using mouse cells, we could not detect any CAR expression in THP-1 cells, while in Jurakt cells their expression was comparable to mCherry transfection rates (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Elimination of CH1-hinge-CH2 subunits did not enable CAR expression in DC2.4 cells.
source: Since myeloid cells were reported to express TRM21 E3 ligases that bind CH1 and CH2 fragments of internalized IgG (Mallery et al., 2010), we next generated a CAR construct with a minimal spacer region by elimination of Constant Heavy domain 1 and 2 (CH1, CH2) and tested the expression of these constructs in DC2.4 cell line. However, consistent with our previous results, we were unable to detect any protein expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-1C.

claim: Removal of all spacer regions did not enable scFv expression in myeloid cells.
source: We then removed the rest of the spacers, generating a construct consisting only of the scFv region and an intracellular signaling domain. As with our previous finding, no expression in myeloid cell lines was detected (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: Removal of the intracellular portion did not alter the expression patterns of TA99-derived scFv.
source: Similarly, removal of the intracellular portion did not alter the expression patterns of TA99-derived scFv, suggesting that the scFv domains may be the element that prevents its expression (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: The scFv domains may be the element that prevents CAR expression in myeloid cells.
source: Similarly, removal of the intracellular portion did not alter the expression patterns of TA99-derived scFv, suggesting that the scFv domains may be the element that prevents its expression (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing that removal of other domains did not restore expression.

claim: Low levels of αCD19-derived scFv were detected but were localized in intracellular compartments and not on the cell membrane.
source: Interestingly, while we detected low levels of αCD19-derived scFv, they were localized in intracellular compartments and not on the cell membrane (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Removal of scFv domain enabled expression of the inserted protein in the Golgi and cell membrane of both macrophages and DC cells.
source: Removal of scFv domain enabled expression of the inserted protein in the Golgi and cell membrane of both macrophages and DC cells (Figure 2H, I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2H, 2I, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Neither TA99- nor αCD19-derived scFv expression was detected intracellularly in DC2.4 cells.
source: Initially, we designed two plasmids in which all other signaling subunits were removed, leaving only the TA99- or αCD19-derived scFv fragment. As with our previous findings, here too we were not able to detect intracellular TA99- nor αCD19-derived scFv expression (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Expression levels of variable light or variable heavy domains alone were somewhat higher than full length scFv, but still benign and significantly lower compared to GFP only.
source: While expression levels were somewhat higher in these constructs, compared to the full length of scFv, they were still benign and significantly lower compared to GFP only (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: Linearization of αCD19 variable light chain had only a marginal effect on its expression patterns and resulted in reduced and compartmentalized expressions.
source: Interestingly, linearization of αCD19 variable light chain (or heavy chain) had only a marginal effect on its expression patterns and resulted in reduced and compartmentalized expressions (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F-H.

claim: Dividing the light chains of αCD19 scFv into three sequences resulted in a high expression in myeloid cells.
source: Dividing the light chains of αCD19 scFv into three sequences resulted in a high expression in myeloid cells, albeit tending to induce different expression patterns of cellular compartmentalization (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: The linear form of either the variable light or the heavy chain of antibodies results in a poor and compartmentalized protein expression compared to the full length of ScFv.
source: Taken jointly, our results suggest that the linear form of either the variable light or the heavy chain of antibodies results in a poor and compartmentalized protein expression compared to the full length of ScFv to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: mRNA transfection of αCD19 scFv-GFP did not lead to expression of scFv in myeloid cells.
source: Nonetheless, this form of transfection did not lead to expression of scFv in myeloid cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Similar levels of GFP mRNA were detected in all transfected cells regardless of construct.
source: Additionally, we measured the mRNA levels of GFP mRNA in mouse myeloid cells following transfection with αCD19 scFv-GFP vectors, in comparison to GFP only or to Fc receptor fused to GFP (which are robustly expressed in these cells). Similar levels of GFP mRNA were detected in all transfected cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The negative regulation on scFv expression is not evident at the mRNA level.
source: Based on these findings, we speculate that the negative regulation on scFv expression is not evident at the mRNA level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mRNA data showing similar levels across constructs.

claim: Only GFP was expressed in myeloid cells from the T2A construct, but not the mCherry which was fused to scFv.
source: While we detected both tags (GFP, mCherry) in HEK293 cells, only GFP was expressed in myeloid cells, but not the mCherry which was fused to scFv (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Eliminating the T2A skipping peptide resulted in abrogated and reduced expression levels of both fluorescent tags in myeloid cells.
source: Eliminating the T2A skipping peptide from this construct, generating a plasmid containing GFP tag fused to TA99 scFv succeeded by mCherry, resulted in abrogated and reduced expression levels of both fluorescent tags in myeloid cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: scFv expression is regulated on the protein level.
source: These results therefore suggest that scFv expression is regulated on the protein level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the T2A experiments showing differential expression of linked proteins.

claim: scFv is expressed in myeloid cell at earlier time points, starting at four hours post-transfection and peaking at about 6 hr.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that scFv is expressed in myeloid cell at earlier time points, starting at four hours post-transfection and peaking at about 6 hr (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: scFv fraction was statistically enriched with proteins associated with ER stress that could promote scFv degradation.
source: Analysis of protein interactors with scFv in myeloid cells indicated that scFv fraction was statistically enriched with proteins associated with ER stress that could promote scFv degradation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The majority of αCD19 scFv were localized at the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Confocal microscopy corroborated that the majority of αCD19 scFv were localized at the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 4G) and co-localized with BIP (Figure 4H) and G3BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which are master regulators of ER stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: αCD19 scFv co-localized with BIP.
source: Confocal microscopy corroborated that the majority of αCD19 scFv were localized at the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 4G) and co-localized with BIP (Figure 4H) and G3BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which are master regulators of ER stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: αCD19 scFv co-localized with G3BP1.
source: Confocal microscopy corroborated that the majority of αCD19 scFv were localized at the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 4G) and co-localized with BIP (Figure 4H) and G3BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which are master regulators of ER stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BIP and G3BP1 are master regulators of ER stress.
source: Confocal microscopy corroborated that the majority of αCD19 scFv were localized at the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 4G) and co-localized with BIP (Figure 4H) and G3BP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), which are master regulators of ER stress.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis indicated higher levels of phospho-JNK in scFv-transfected cells.
source: Lastly, flow cytometric analysis indicated higher levels of phospho-JNK (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Alpha chain from TRP1-reactive TCR could not be expressed following transfection of RAW264.7 cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, we could not detect expression of alpha chain from TRP1-reactive TCR Dougan et al., 2013 following transfection of RAW264.7 cells (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both naive and chimeric FcγRI constructs were successfully expressed at comparable levels in RAW264.7 cells.
source: Flow cytometric analysis 24 hr post-transfection indicated that both constructs were successfully expressed at comparable levels (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Both naive and chimeric FcγRI constructs expressed on the cell membrane and Golgi.
source: Confocal microscopy further indicated that both constructs expressed on the cell membrane and Golgi. (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RAW264.7 alone had no cytotoxic activity following a 24 hr incubation with tumor cells.
source: Confocal microscopy indicated that RAW264.7 alone had no cytotoxic activity following a 24 hr incubation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The addition of trastuzumab induced a polarized accumulation of GrB in the synapse between macrophages and tumor cells.
source: In contrast, the addition of trastuzumab induced a polarized accumulation of GrB in the synapse between macrophages and tumor cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Significantly higher levels of GrB in the immune synapse were counted in cells expressing C5aR chimeric receptor.
source: Significantly higher levels of GrB in the immune synapse were counted in cells expressing C5aR chimeric receptor (Figure 5F, G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5F, 5G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transfected macrophages alone were almost completely inert whereas the addition of trastuzumab promoted tumor cell killing.
source: Consistent with GrB polarization, transfected macrophages alone were almost completely inert whereas the addition of trastuzumab promoted tumor cell killing (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by IncuCyte data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Killing rates of macrophages expressing C5aR chimeric receptor were higher, but were also induced by free and irrelevant antibody.
source: Importantly, while killing rates of macrophages expressing C5aR chimeric receptor were higher, they were also induced by free and irrelevant antibody (e.g. rituximab; Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by IncuCyte data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cells transfected with the native FcγRI had a clear separation between the alpha chain and their signaling gamma chain in steady state.
source: In steady state, cells transfected with the native FcγRI had a clear separation between the alpha chain (antibody binding chain) and their signaling gamma chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The addition of free trastuzumab did not alter the membranal architecture of native FcγRI.
source: The addition of free trastuzumab did not alter their membranal architecture.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Incubation with plastic-immobilized trastuzumab resulted in polarization of the alpha chain toward the plastic and co-localization with the gamma chain.
source: Incubation with plastic-immobilized trastuzumab resulted in polarization of the alpha chain toward the plastic and co-localization with the gamma chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The architecture of C5aR chimeric receptor completely abrogated the membrane organization of the signaling chains, as the two co-localized even under steady state.
source: The architecture of C5aR chimeric receptor completely abrogated the membrane organization of the signaling chains, as the two co-localized even under steady state (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The IgM receptor signaling chain construct can be highly expressed in macrophage membrane.
source: Indeed, this architecture can be highly expressed in macrophage membrane and did not recruit or abrogate the gamma chain upon addition of antibodies, while maintaining alpha chain clustering to immobilized trastuzumab (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-1F.

claim: The IgM receptor signaling chain construct did not recruit or abrogate the gamma chain upon addition of antibodies.
source: Indeed, this architecture can be highly expressed in macrophage membrane and did not recruit or abrogate the gamma chain upon addition of antibodies, while maintaining alpha chain clustering to immobilized trastuzumab (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-1F.

claim: The IgM receptor signaling chain construct maintained alpha chain clustering to immobilized trastuzumab.
source: Indeed, this architecture can be highly expressed in macrophage membrane and did not recruit or abrogate the gamma chain upon addition of antibodies, while maintaining alpha chain clustering to immobilized trastuzumab (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-1F.

claim: The IgM receptor signaling chain construct promotes polarized expression of GrB at the immunological synapse and induces an antibody-specific tumor cell lysis.
source: This construct promotes polarized expression of GrB at the immunological synapse and induces an antibody-specific tumor cell lysis (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Significant inhibition of tumor growth was observed in mice treated with modified FcγRI and TA99, but not with sham transfected BMDC or without TA99 antibodies.
source: Indeed, significant inhibition of tumor growth was observed in mice treated with modified FcγRI and TA99, but not with sham transfected BMDC or without TA99 antibodies (Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-1I.

claim: Higher rates of T cells were found in tumors treated with modified DC and TA99.
source: Analysis of immune cell infiltration indicated higher rates of T cells in tumors treated with modified DC and TA99. (Figure 5L) suggesting this treatment also potentiate the hosts immune response.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Treatment with modified DC and TA99 potentiates the host's immune response.
source: Analysis of immune cell infiltration indicated higher rates of T cells in tumors treated with modified DC and TA99. (Figure 5L) suggesting this treatment also potentiate the hosts immune response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased T cell infiltration data.

claim: The microenvironment of most solid tumors is often enriched with myeloid cells at different stages of maturity and polarization.
source: The microenvironment of most solid tumors is often enriched with myeloid cells at different stages of maturity and polarization and the general notion suggests that they often adopt a suppressive phenotype that supports tumor progression and escape (Bruni et al., 2020; Mantovani and Sica, 2010; Gajewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells often adopt a suppressive phenotype that supports tumor progression and escape.
source: The microenvironment of most solid tumors is often enriched with myeloid cells at different stages of maturity and polarization and the general notion suggests that they often adopt a suppressive phenotype that supports tumor progression and escape (Bruni et al., 2020; Mantovani and Sica, 2010; Gajewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The inherent plasticity of myeloid cells enables them to change their phenotype upon injection of adjuvant or immune-stimulatory agents.
source: The inherent plasticity of these cells, however, enables them to change their phenotype upon injection of adjuvant or immune-stimulatory agents (Quatromoni and Eruslanov, 2012; Ricketts et al., 2021; Bercovici et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most attempts to convert tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells phenotype to an anti-tumor phenotype did not meet expectations.
source: While they showed improved T cell infiltration and overall lower tumor burden, they did not meet the expectations.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of prior experimental and clinical data.

claim: Most attempts to activate myeloid cells are based on the notion that CD8+ T cells are the main effector arm against cancer and that the purpose of myeloid cell activation is to support T cell-mediated killing.
source: It is noteworthy that most of these attempts are based on the notion that CD8+ T cells are the main effector arm against cancer and that the purpose of myeloid cell activation is to support T cell-mediated killing (Ricketts et al., 2021; Bercovici et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myeloid cells are highly equipped with cell-killing mechanisms, including antibody-medicated cellular toxicity (ADCC) and secretion of reactive oxygen species.
source: Nonetheless, myeloid cells are highly equipped with cell-killing mechanisms, including antibody-medicated cellular toxicity (ADCC) and secretion of reactive oxygen species (Mantovani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activating the IgM-receptor signaling in myeloid cells using tumor-binding IgG induces oxidative burst, Granzyme release, and massive tumor cell lysis.
source: Here, we demonstrated that activating the IgM-receptor signaling in myeloid cells using tumor-binding IgG induces oxidative burst, Granzyme release, and massive tumor cell lysis.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the study.

claim: Cells of the myeloid lineage resist gene modification.
source: While genetic engineering of immune cells to treat cancer has proven to be successful in lymphoid cells (Gross and Eshhar, 2016; Kalos et al., 2011), cells of the myeloid lineage resist gene modification.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Myeloid cells are traditionally thought to be programmed to respond to foreign genetic materials.
source: Noteworthily, these cells are traditionally thought to be programmed to respond to foreign genetic materials.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Biglari et al. demonstrated that the fusion of scFv against CEA to FcγR can be expressed in monocytes using adenoviral vectors.
source: Early attempts to overcome this inherent barrier were achieved by Biglari et al. using adenoviral vectors. They demonstrated that the fusion of scFv against CEA to FcγR can be expressed in monocytes (Biglari et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Most CAR receptors designed by Morrissey et al. do not appear to be expressed on the cell membrane.
source: Interestingly, most of these receptors do not appear to be expressed on the cell membrane.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work by Morrissey et al.

claim: CAR-merTK, which appears on the cell membrane, was functionally inert and did not induce phagocytosis.
source: Moreover, CAR-merTK, which appears on the cell membrane, was functionally inert and did not induce phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work by Morrissey et al.

claim: Klichinsky et al. concluded that the improved survival induced in mice was due to M1-like phenotype induced in transduced macrophages by the virus, rather than the CAR construct.
source: With that being said, the authors concluded that the improved survival induced in mice was due to M1-like phenotype induced in transduced macrophages by the virus, rather than the CAR construct (Klichinsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.
